nature-pol-314.title: Perverse incentives and the cobra effect
nature-pol-314.text:
In Hanoi in 1902, a bounty paid 1 cent per rat tail. Rat catchers cut off the tails and released the rats to breed more. A perverse incentive is a structure that produces undesirable results, especially effects unexpected and contrary to what its designers intended. Horst Siebert coined the name "cobra effect" in 2001 from a British Raj anecdote about a bounty on dead cobras. That anecdote is disputed: a 2025 investigation found no contemporary records of cobra breeding in British India, said the Madras bounty was scaled back over cost, not fraud, and urged retiring the term.

Other cases hold up better. At Fort Benning a $40 bounty per feral pig tail coincided with a rising pig population; feed bait raised fertility and survival, and hunters preferred large males over females and juveniles. Endangered Species Act restrictions on landowners can encourage preemptive habitat destruction. A carbon credit scheme gave one of the highest bounties for destroying the refrigerant byproduct HFC-23, so firms made more refrigerant to earn credits; the EU suspended such credits in 2013. Grandfathered emission permits, offsets, Clean Development Mechanism credits and subsidised flood insurance have all drawn the same criticism.

nature-pol-315.title: The right to know about hazards
nature-pol-315.text: The right to know is the right of people to know about hazards and substances that may harm them, often framed around chemicals. UNESCO defines it as letting people take part in decisions that affect them in an informed way while holding governments and others accountable. In the United States it takes two forms, Community Right to Know and Workplace Right to Know, and appears in Rachel Carson's Silent Spring. The Bhopal disaster of December 1984, in which a methyl isocyanate cloud killed 2,000 people, drove the push for more hazard information. The Hazard Communication Standard, in force from 1985, makes manufacturers and employers tell workers about chemical hazards, and the 1986 Emergency Planning and Right to Know Act followed.

nature-pol-290.title: How climate change denial works
nature-pol-290.text:
Climate change denial is a form of science denial. It rejects, disputes or fights the extensive evidence for human-caused global warming and the scientific consensus on it. Those promoting it use rhetorical tactics to make a scientific controversy appear where none exists: raising unreasonable doubt about human causes and effects, and understating adaptation costs while overstating the costs of mitigation. Its tactics include delaying mitigation, pushing adaptation only, disputing IPCC processes, and promoting conspiracy theories.

The downplaying approach was copied from tobacco lobbyists, who tried to prevent or delay regulation despite scientific evidence linking tobacco to lung cancer. ExxonMobil led climate change denial from the 1980s to the mid 2000s and helped prevent US ratification of the Kyoto Protocol; research found its scientific opinion and public posture contradicted each other. A 2008 University of Central Florida study found that 92% of environmentally skeptical literature published in the US was partly or wholly affiliated with conservative think tanks.

The campaigns have lowered public belief in climate change, which has affected legislative efforts to curb CO2 emissions. As of February 2024, at least 32 US lawsuits sought damages from the fossil fuel industry for spreading denial despite knowing the risks.

nature-pol-292.title: Advocacy groups and their influence
nature-pol-292.text:
Advocacy groups, also called lobby groups, interest groups or pressure groups, use advocacy or lobbying to influence political and social systems. They use media campaigns, publicity stunts, polls, research and policy briefings to pursue their aims. Some are backed by powerful business or political interests, while others have few resources; poorer groups may turn to direct action and civil disobedience.

In liberal democracies groups mainly work through the bureaucracy, where decision-making power lies, but access is generally limited to insiders such as large corporations and trade unions. Groups with more money are generally better able to influence government decisions, and large businesses gain from being key producers whose contributions matter to the economy. Pluralism sees groups competing and acting as a counterweight to undue concentrations of power; neo-pluralism organises groups around a government department and its client groups. Lobbying is regulated to stop the worst abuses, which can develop into corruption.

nature-pol-288.title: Network effects: value that grows with users
nature-pol-288.text: A network effect is when the value a user gets from a good or service depends on how many users of compatible products there are. Usually it is a positive feedback system: each added user raises the value for those already in the network. Growth is not endless, since a network tends to plateau at market saturation or when reaching the last customers becomes prohibitively costly. Returns are not always proportional either; they depend on commoditization of supply, the type of added user and the substitutes available. Network effects often yield multiple equilibria, and expectations, shaped by path dependence such as first-mover advantage, decide which appears and can produce lock-in.

nature-pol-291.title: Why people deny climate change
nature-pol-291.text: The psychology of climate change denial studies why people deny climate change despite the scientific consensus. One study identified seven psychological barriers to mitigation, adaptation and stewardship, including cognition, ideological worldviews, disbelief in experts, costs and perceived risks of change. Denial is not simply overcome by reasoned argument, and supplying missing information or general science education may be ineffective. Explaining techniques such as cherrypicking, fake experts and false balance has been shown to inoculate people somewhat against misinformation.

nature-pol-293.title: Why people join interest groups
nature-pol-293.text: Everyone gains from a cleaner environment, yet environmental groups do not get money from everyone. That is the free rider problem: members are hard to recruit when the benefits are enjoyed without joining. Groups therefore rely on a mix of enticements. Selective benefits are material rewards to members, such as discounted travel, meals or subscriptions. Solidarity incentives are socially derived rewards of association, such as group identity and status. Expressive incentives reward members for voicing a value they believe in, whether or not the goal is achieved; environmental and public-interest groups rely on them.

nature-pol-289.title: Market tipping and winner-take-all markets
nature-pol-289.text: Market tipping is the tendency of one system to pull away from its rivals in popularity once it has gained an initial edge. It happens because network effects give users an incentive to coordinate their adoption on a single product, a natural form of market concentration. The result is one good or service dominant, competition stifled, and sometimes monopoly.

nature-pol-321.title: Tariffs: taxes on imports
nature-pol-321.text:
From 1790 to 1860, import duties made up about 90% of US federal receipts. A tariff is a duty imposed by a national government or union on imported goods, paid by the importer. Besides raising revenue, it regulates foreign trade by burdening foreign products to encourage or safeguard domestic industry. Douglas Irwin says tariffs have served three purposes: revenue, protection of domestic producers, and securing reciprocity through trade agreements. Protective tariffs are among the most widely used tools of protectionism, along with import and export quotas and other non-tariff barriers.

Economic analyses generally find that tariffs distort the free market and raise prices of both foreign and domestic products. Welfare effects on the importing country are usually negative even without retaliation. The 1930 Smoot-Hawley act raised the average tariff on dutiable imports from about 40% to 47%. Duty is often charged ad valorem on a transaction value, with goods identified by Harmonized System codes developed by the World Customs Organization.

nature-pol-325.title: Foreign direct investment and control
nature-pol-325.text:
Foreign direct investment is a controlling ownership stake in a company or asset in one country held by an investor, firm or government from another. Control separates it from foreign portfolio investment, a passive holding of foreign stocks and bonds. The World Bank's narrow definition is a lasting management interest of 10% or more of voting stock in an enterprise abroad. Broadly it covers mergers and acquisitions, new facilities, reinvested profits and intracompany loans, and usually involves management participation and transfer of technology and expertise.

Before Stephen Hymer's 1960 work no theory dealt specifically with it; Heckscher and Ohlin's factor-proportions logic had treated foreign investment generally. A 2010 meta-analysis found it robustly raises local firms' productivity growth in developing and transition countries. Incentives to attract it include low corporate and income tax rates and exemptions from regulations, usually for very large projects.

nature-pol-324.title: The environmental dumping argument
nature-pol-324.text: Firms may gain unfair competition from weaker environmental regulation elsewhere. That is the argument for tariffs called environmental dumping. The EU starts its carbon border-adjustment mechanism in 2026 to level the playing field with firms not subject to European carbon pricing.

nature-pol-323.title: The infant industry argument for protection
nature-pol-323.text: Emerging industries, especially in less-developed countries, may need temporary protection from established foreign competitors. Mainstream economists accept that tariffs can help industries develop in the short term, but this depends on the protection being temporary and on the government's ability to manage it. Most economists, following comparative advantage, argue that struggling industries should not be maintained by protection. So the question stays contested: protectionists argue for temporary protection, while most economists doubt it works.

nature-pol-322.title: The optimal tariff
nature-pol-322.text: An optimal tariff is one set to maximise the welfare of the country imposing it. Free trade is often the best policy for efficiency, but levying a tariff is sometimes second best.

nature-pol-326.title: Types of foreign direct investment
nature-pol-326.text: Foreign direct investment can be sorted two ways. From the investor's view it is horizontal, vertical or conglomerate. Horizontal investment duplicates a multinational's home industry chain in the destination country to make similar goods. Vertical investment buys a firm to exploit natural resources in the host country, which is backward, or distribution outlets to market its products there, which is forward. Conglomerate investment combines horizontal and vertical; platform investment invests in one country to export to a third. From the host country's view the classes are import-substituting, export-increasing and government-initiated.

nature-mkt-153.title: Debt: what is owed and how it is repaid
nature-mkt-153.text:
Debt is an obligation to repay money borrowed or otherwise owed to another party. It can be owed by a country, local government, company or individual, and loans, bonds, notes and mortgages are all forms of it. Repayment may be structured as the whole principal due at maturity, amortized over the loan term, or partly amortized with the rest due at the end. A debt is secured if creditors can claim specific collateral; unsecured debt gives them no recourse to the borrower's assets.

Governments issue debt for ongoing expenses and capital projects, and show their overall indebtedness as a debt-to-GDP ratio. Rating agencies such as Moody's, Standard & Poor's and Fitch grade debt by the debtor's ability to honour it. Bonds are tradeable debt securities, while loans are not, though securitization can turn loans into them. Debt is denominated in a currency, so inflation or deflation can change its effective size even when borrower and lender use the same currency.

nature-mkt-154.title: Divestment and the fossil fuel campaign
nature-mkt-154.text: Divestment is the reduction of an asset, or the sale of a business, for financial, ethical or political objectives. Firms divest to focus on core operations, raise cash, stabilise results, drop failing units, or comply with regulators. Shareholder pressure for social reasons is often called disinvestment, and has targeted apartheid South Africa, tobacco, factory farming and fossil fuels, the last coordinated by 350.org since the 2010s. As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions holding over $40.5 trillion had begun or committed to some fossil fuel divestment. Financial research suggests it has raised investors' returns in the longer term.

nature-res-274.title: Exchange rates: one currency in another
nature-res-274.text: An interbank rate of 141 yen to the dollar means 141 yen buy one US dollar. That is an exchange rate, the rate at which one currency is exchanged for another. Countries choose a regime: free-floating, set by supply and demand, pegged or fixed, or a hybrid. A currency gains value when demand for it exceeds supply and loses value when demand falls short. A country may hold its currency low to gain a trade advantage, which cheapens its exports abroad but raises the price of imports at home. Under the balance of payments model, a trade deficit shrinks foreign exchange reserves and depreciates the currency; a cheaper currency then lifts exports, cuts imports and moves the trade balance back toward equilibrium.

nature-res-275.title: The real exchange rate and competitiveness
nature-res-275.text: The real exchange rate is the purchasing power of one currency relative to another at current exchange rates and prices: the nominal rate times the relative price of a market basket of goods in the two countries. It reflects a country's competitiveness against the rest of the world. Currency appreciation or high domestic inflation lowers it, which reduces competitiveness and the current account; depreciation has the opposite effect. A bilateral rate covers one currency pair, while an effective rate is a weighted average over a basket of foreign currencies and serves as an overall measure of external competitiveness.

nature-res-255.title: Total allowable catch and the race for fish
nature-res-255.text: In the Alaskan halibut fishery the race became so extreme that the season shrank to a single 24-hour dash, and perishable fish were landed in a clump. The cause was a total allowable catch, a cap on the catch of a whole fishery: fishers may fish when and how they like until the quota is met, then fishing stops until the next season. The cap does not remove the underlying competition among fishers for the fish. It often produces overcapitalization of the industry and races between boat crews to land fish before the quota runs out. The EU Common Fisheries Policy sets such caps per species and ICES area, yearly or two-yearly, and gives each country a quota from its traditional percentage share.

nature-res-256.title: The EU Common Fisheries Policy
nature-res-256.text:
The Common Fisheries Policy is the European Union's fisheries policy: it sets catch quotas, gives member states access to one another's exclusive economic zones and manages sustainable fishing in the EU's zone. Member states may implement its principles through licences, limited entry or individual fishing quota, and regulations cover gear and closed areas. Enforcement is left to member states, with a community inspection service checking them. The 2013 reform, in force from 1 January 2014, was meant to protect endangered stocks and end discards, with maximum sustainable yield to apply from 2015.

Critics say per-species quotas force fish to be thrown overboard dead, and that its centralised top-down approach should give way to participatory governance. Commentators disagree on whether the policy harmed stocks or merely failed to reverse a decline that predated it. A 2010 study traced stock depletion to mismanagement long before the policy, with British catch rates down 94% over 118 years.
